title: Evidence of Evolution and Common Ancestry
subject: AP Biology
objectives: Describe how the fossil record and transitional fossils document evolutionary change over time
Distinguish homologous, analogous, and vestigial structures and explain what each reveals about ancestry
Explain how molecular and developmental evidence (DNA, proteins, embryology) supports common ancestry
Interpret multiple independent lines of evidence as converging support for evolution

sections.heading: A Case Built From Many Independent Witnesses
sections.content:
When a detective builds a case, no single clue convicts — but when fingerprints, DNA, a motive, and an eyewitness ALL point to the same conclusion independently, the case becomes overwhelming. Evolution is exactly this kind of case. It isn't supported by one type of evidence but by many completely independent lines — fossils, anatomy, molecules, embryos, and observed change — that were gathered by different scientists using different methods, yet all converge on the same story: living things share common ancestors and have changed over time. That convergence from independent directions is what makes evolution one of the best-supported ideas in all of science.

The central concept tying the evidence together is common ancestry: the idea that different species descend from shared ancestors, like cousins tracing back to the same grandparents. The more recently two species shared an ancestor, the more features they should share. So evidence for evolution is, at heart, evidence that organisms are related — and relatedness leaves fingerprints in bones, body plans, DNA sequences, and embryos.

This lesson surveys those lines of evidence. As you go, notice the recurring logic: shared features inherited from a common ancestor (homology) reveal relatedness, while features that merely LOOK similar because of similar environments (analogy) do not. Telling those two apart is the key skill the AP exam tests here.

sections.heading: Fossils and the Record of Change Over Time
sections.content:
Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of organisms from the past, and together they form the fossil record — a physical timeline of life. Because sedimentary rock builds up in layers (strata) over time, deeper layers are generally older and shallower layers younger, so fossils can be ordered in time. Radiometric dating, which measures the predictable decay of radioactive isotopes, puts absolute ages on rocks and fossils. The record shows unmistakable change: the organisms in ancient rocks differ from those in recent rocks, simpler forms generally appear before complex ones, and many species that once existed are now extinct.

The most striking fossil evidence is transitional fossils — forms that show intermediate features linking major groups. Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fossil, has features of both fish and early four-legged animals (gills and scales like a fish, but also a flat head, neck, and sturdy fin-bones like a limb) — a snapshot of vertebrates moving onto land. Archaeopteryx blends reptilian features (teeth, a bony tail, clawed fingers) with bird features (feathers, wings). A series of whale fossils traces sea-dwelling whales back to four-legged land mammals, complete with shrinking hind limbs. These intermediates are exactly what common ancestry predicts.

A caution the exam likes: the fossil record is INCOMPLETE — fossilization is rare and requires special conditions, so most organisms never fossilized and many fossils remain undiscovered. Gaps in the record reflect this rarity, not a failure of evolution; and the gaps keep being filled as new fossils (like Tiktaalik, found by predicting where to look) are unearthed.

sections.question: Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fossil, has gills and scales like a fish but also a flat head, neck, and sturdy limb-like fin bones. Why is it considered strong evidence for evolution?
options: It proves fish are turning into amphibians today
It is a transitional fossil showing intermediate features that link fish to early four-legged land vertebrates, as common ancestry predicts
It shows that individual fish can grow legs during their lifetimes
It is the direct ancestor of all living humans
sections.explanation: Tiktaalik is a transitional fossil: it combines features of fish and of early tetrapods, documenting the kind of intermediate form predicted if land vertebrates descended from fish ancestors. It does not show living fish changing today, individuals growing legs in a lifetime, or a direct line to humans — it is a snapshot of an evolutionary transition in the deep past.

sections.heading: Anatomical Evidence: Homology, Analogy, and Vestigial Structures
sections.content:
Comparing the bodies of different species reveals patterns that only common ancestry explains well. Homologous structures are features that share the same underlying structure and developmental origin because they were inherited from a common ancestor — even if they now do different jobs. The classic example is the vertebrate forelimb: a human arm, a whale flipper, a bat wing, and a cat leg all contain the SAME set of bones in the same arrangement (one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones, digits), despite being used for grasping, swimming, flying, and walking. Same blueprint, different functions — exactly what you'd expect if all descended from a common ancestor whose limb was modified for different lifestyles.

Contrast this with analogous structures: features that look similar and do similar jobs but evolved INDEPENDENTLY in unrelated lineages, with different underlying structure. A bird's wing and an insect's wing both enable flight but are built completely differently and share no winged common ancestor. Analogy arises from convergent evolution — different lineages independently evolving similar solutions to similar environmental challenges (streamlined shapes in sharks, dolphins, and ichthyosaurs, for instance). The crucial exam distinction: HOMOLOGY (shared ancestry, similar structure) reveals relatedness; ANALOGY (similar function, different structure) does NOT — it reflects similar selection pressures, not a recent common ancestor.

Vestigial structures are reduced, seemingly functionless remnants of features that were useful in an ancestor — the human appendix and tailbone, the tiny hip and leg bones buried in whales and some snakes, eyes in blind cave fish. They make sense only as leftovers of an evolutionary past: why would an organism be 'designed' with the useless remains of a structure its relatives use fully? They're homologous structures caught in the act of being lost.

sections.heading: Reading Anatomical Evidence
rows: Inherited from a common ancestor (divergent evolution)
Similar selection pressures, NOT close relatedness
Reduced remnant of an ancestral structure
Loss of function over evolutionary time
Descent with modification from an ancestor that used it

sections.heading: Molecular and Developmental Evidence
sections.content:
The most powerful modern evidence comes from molecules. Because all life uses the SAME DNA-based genetic code (Unit 6) and many of the same core proteins, we can compare the actual genetic sequences of different species — and the pattern is exactly what common ancestry predicts. Closely related species have very similar DNA and protein sequences; distantly related species differ more. Humans and chimpanzees share roughly 98–99% of their DNA; humans and mice less; humans and yeast less still — but we share with yeast the genes for basic processes like cellular respiration, because we inherited them from a very ancient common ancestor. Universal features — the same genetic code, the same ATP energy currency, ribosomes in every cell — point to a single origin of life.

Molecular differences also act as a clock. Because mutations accumulate over time at a roughly steady rate, the NUMBER of sequence differences between two species estimates how long ago they diverged: more differences, more time since their common ancestor. This 'molecular clock' lets biologists build and date evolutionary trees from DNA alone, and it independently agrees with trees built from fossils and anatomy — different methods, same answer.

Developmental (embryological) evidence rounds out the case. Vertebrate embryos — fish, chicken, human — look strikingly similar in early development, all showing features like pharyngeal (gill) pouches and tails, because they share the same ancient developmental genes (including the Hox genes from Unit 6) inherited from a common ancestor. The shared toolkit of developmental genes across wildly different animals is itself strong evidence of deep common ancestry.

sections.heading: Using Molecular Data to Infer Relatedness
sections.content:
A common exam task gives you a table of molecular differences and asks which species are most closely related. Suppose you're told the number of amino-acid differences in a shared protein (say, a hemoglobin chain) between humans and several other species:

  Human vs. chimpanzee: 0 differences
  Human vs. gorilla: 1 difference
  Human vs. mouse: 27 differences
  Human vs. frog: 67 differences

Step 1 — Apply the core principle: FEWER molecular differences mean a MORE RECENT common ancestor (more closely related); MORE differences mean a more distant common ancestor.

Step 2 — Rank by similarity to humans. Chimpanzee (0) is most similar, then gorilla (1), then mouse (27), then frog (67). So the order of relatedness to humans, closest to most distant, is chimp → gorilla → mouse → frog.

Step 3 — Translate into a tree/ancestry statement. Humans and chimps share the most recent common ancestor; the human-frog common ancestor is the most ancient. On a phylogenetic tree (next lesson), chimp would branch from the human line most recently and frog the earliest.

Step 4 — Reason about the molecular clock. Because differences accumulate roughly with time, the 67 human-frog differences imply far more time since divergence than the 1 human-gorilla difference. The exam reward is stating the rule explicitly — 'fewer differences = more recent common ancestor = more closely related' — and using it consistently. Watch the trap: more differences does NOT mean 'more evolved' or 'more primitive,' just more time since the lineages split.

sections.heading: Deciding Whether Similar Features Show Relatedness

steps.title: Look past function to underlying structure
steps.content: Don't be fooled by what a structure DOES. Examine the underlying anatomy and developmental origin. A bat wing and a bird wing both fly, but you must check whether the bones and development match.

steps.title: Same structure, different function → homologous
steps.content: If the features share the same underlying parts and developmental origin (like the one-bone/two-bone/digits pattern of vertebrate limbs), they are homologous — inherited from a common ancestor. This DOES indicate relatedness.

steps.title: Similar function, different structure → analogous
steps.content: If the features do a similar job but are built differently (a bird wing vs. an insect wing), they are analogous, the product of convergent evolution under similar selection pressures. This does NOT indicate close relatedness.

steps.title: Corroborate with independent evidence
steps.content: Check whether molecular (DNA/protein), fossil, and developmental data agree. When multiple independent lines point to the same relationships, the inference of common ancestry is strong. Conflicting analogy is filtered out this way.

sections.question: A dolphin (a mammal) and a shark (a fish) both have streamlined bodies and fins for fast swimming, but their internal anatomy and development differ greatly. These similar features are best described as...
options: homologous structures showing they are closely related
analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution under similar selection pressures
evidence that dolphins evolved from sharks
sections.explanation: Streamlined bodies in dolphins and sharks are analogous structures: they serve a similar function (fast swimming) but evolved independently in distantly related lineages facing the same selective pressure (moving efficiently through water). This is convergent evolution. The similarity reflects shared environment, not close relatedness — homology would require shared underlying structure and ancestry.

sections.content: Independent lines of evidence — fossils (including transitional forms), homologous structures, vestigial structures, molecular sequence comparisons, and embryology — all converge on common ancestry. Homologous structures (same structure, often different function) reveal relatedness, while analogous structures (similar function, different structure) reflect convergent evolution, not close kinship; and fewer molecular differences mean a more recent common ancestor.

sections.heading: Evidence Misconceptions to Avoid
sections.content: (1) HOMOLOGOUS = shared ancestry (same structure, maybe different function); ANALOGOUS = convergent evolution (similar function, different structure). Don't swap them — a bat wing and human arm are homologous; a bat wing and insect wing are analogous. (2) Vestigial structures are reduced/non-functional REMNANTS, not 'unfinished' new structures. (3) Fewer molecular differences = MORE closely related (more recent common ancestor) — not 'more evolved.' (4) An incomplete fossil record (gaps) reflects how rare fossilization is, NOT a flaw in evolution. (5) Transitional fossils are intermediates between groups, not living things changing today. (6) No single species in a comparison is 'more evolved' or 'higher' — all living species have been evolving for the same amount of time.

sections.heading: When a Prediction Comes True: The Power of Convergent Evidence
sections.content:
What makes the evidence for evolution scientifically powerful is not just its quantity but that the theory makes RISKY, testable predictions — and they keep coming true. Consider Tiktaalik. Paleontologists reasoned that if four-limbed land animals evolved from fish, an intermediate should exist in rocks of a particular age (~375 million years) laid down in the right shallow-water environment. They went to Arctic Canada to rocks of exactly that age and, after years of searching, found Tiktaalik — a creature with the predicted fish-tetrapod blend, in the predicted time and place. A theory that lets you predict where to dig for a fossil that nobody had ever seen is doing exactly what good science should. Evolution also predicted, before DNA sequencing existed, that molecular data should produce the SAME family tree as anatomy and fossils — and when sequencing arrived, it largely did, an independent confirmation Darwin never could have engineered.

This convergence is the heart of the matter. Fossils are dated by physics (radiometric decay), anatomy is compared by structure, molecules are compared by sequence, and embryos by development — utterly different methods, run by different specialists, with no way to coordinate their answers. Yet they agree: whales group with mammals (their vestigial hip bones, their mammalian DNA, their fossil land-dwelling ancestors all concur); humans group with other primates by bones, by genes, by shared retroviral DNA insertions, and by embryology alike. When independent methods that could easily have contradicted each other instead converge, the conclusion they share becomes extraordinarily robust.

The evidence is also profoundly unifying — it connects every unit you've studied. The universal genetic code and shared core proteins (Unit 6) ARE molecular evidence of a single origin of life. The Hox genes that pattern embryos (Unit 6) are the developmental evidence. The homologous biochemistry of respiration and photosynthesis (Unit 3) shows our kinship with bacteria and plants. Even the mutations and allele-frequency changes of the previous lessons are the very mechanism that, run over deep time, produced the branching tree these lines of evidence reveal. Common ancestry isn't a separate fact bolted onto biology; it's the framework that makes the whole subject cohere — which is why the next lesson turns this evidence into the actual tree of life: phylogeny.

sections.heading: How AP Tests Evidence for Evolution
sections.content: Point-winners: (1) Classify structures as homologous (relatedness), analogous (convergent evolution), or vestigial, and state what each implies. (2) From molecular-difference data, rank relatedness using 'fewer differences = more recent common ancestor' and translate it into ancestry/tree statements (sets up phylogeny). (3) Explain WHY multiple independent lines converging is powerful evidence. (4) Interpret the fossil record (strata = relative age, transitional fossils as intermediates) and explain that gaps reflect rare fossilization. (5) Use molecular/developmental universals (genetic code, Hox genes, shared embryonic features) as evidence of common ancestry. (6) Avoid 'more evolved/higher/primitive' language; describe relatedness by recency of common ancestor.

aiContext: This AP Biology Unit 7 lesson covers the evidence for evolution and common ancestry (CED topics 7.7-7.9). Frame it as a convergent case: many INDEPENDENT lines of evidence — fossils, anatomy, molecules, embryology, and directly observed change — all point to common ancestry (species descending from shared ancestors), and that independent convergence is what makes evolution one of the best-supported ideas in science. Fossil evidence: the fossil record orders life in time (deeper strata older; radiometric dating gives absolute ages), shows change over time and extinction, and includes TRANSITIONAL fossils with intermediate features (Tiktaalik = fish-to-tetrapod, Archaeopteryx = reptile-to-bird, whale series = land-mammal-to-whale); gaps reflect the RARITY of fossilization, not a flaw in evolution. Anatomical evidence centers on the most-tested distinction: HOMOLOGOUS structures share underlying structure and developmental origin from a common ancestor (vertebrate forelimb: human arm, whale flipper, bat wing, cat leg — same bones, different functions) and INDICATE relatedness (divergent evolution); ANALOGOUS structures have similar function but different structure, evolved independently (bird wing vs. insect wing; dolphin vs. shark streamlining) via CONVERGENT evolution and do NOT indicate close relatedness; VESTIGIAL structures are reduced remnants of ancestral features (appendix, whale hip bones, cave-fish eyes). Molecular evidence: all life shares the genetic code and core proteins (Unit 6), and sequence similarity tracks relatedness — FEWER differences mean a MORE RECENT common ancestor (humans ~98-99% DNA with chimps); the molecular clock dates divergences and independently agrees with fossil/anatomical trees. Developmental evidence: vertebrate embryos share features (pharyngeal pouches, tails) and the same Hox developmental genes. Key misconceptions to counter: swapping homologous/analogous, calling species 'more evolved/higher/primitive,' reading more molecular differences as 'more advanced' rather than 'more time since divergence,' and treating fossil gaps as evidence against evolution. Students must do molecular-data ranking problems (fewer differences = closer relative), classify structures, and explain why independent converging evidence is compelling. Connects to Unit 6 (universal code, Hox genes), Unit 3 (shared biochemistry), and forward to phylogeny (turning this evidence into trees).
